planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; set a second seedling or named cultivar nearby, since Eaton is not reliably self-fruitful.

directions: Eaton is a Chinese chestnut selection valued for consistently large, sweet, easy-to-peel nuts on a productive, comparatively fast-bearing tree. Like other Chinese chestnuts it carries strong resistance to chestnut blight, letting it thrive in regions where the related American chestnut has vanished. Give it deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun and plant a genetically distinct pollinizer within a hundred feet or so for a full crop. Harvest burs as they split open and drop in early fall, and gather promptly since fallen nuts spoil quickly and attract wildlife.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry
Northern Nut Growers Association
USDA Agricultural Research Service

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in deep, well-drained loam in full sun; plant a compatible pollinizer such as 'Wepster' or 'York' nearby, since hazelnuts are self-incompatible.

directions: Dorris was released by the Oregon State University hazelnut breeding program with strong resistance to eastern filbert blight, the disease that devastated older European cultivars across the Pacific Northwest. It bears large, round, high-quality kernels on a vigorous, upright tree and ripens in the midseason window alongside cultivars like Jefferson. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible blight-resistant pollinizer nearby, since hazelnuts will not set a crop alone. Harvest begins once nuts drop free of the husk in early fall; gather promptly from the ground to beat squirrels and reduce mold risk.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Hazelnut Cultivars
Oregon Hazelnut Industry Office
Nut Growers Society of Oregon, Washington and British Columbia

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in deep, well-drained loam in full sun, primarily as a pollinizer paired with a main-crop cultivar like Jefferson or Dorris.

directions: York is an Oregon State University-released hazelnut selected mainly as a compatible pollinizer for eastern-filbert-blight-resistant orchard cultivars, shedding pollen over a long, late window that overlaps well with modern main-crop bloom times. It also carries strong blight resistance itself and produces a respectable crop of good-quality, medium-sized kernels in its own right, not just pollen. Grow it exactly as other hazelnuts, in deep, well-drained soil and full sun, and prune out root suckers each year to keep the tree in a single-trunk or multi-stem form rather than a thicket. Harvest as nuts drop free of the husk in early fall.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Hazelnut Cultivars
Oregon Hazelnut Industry Office

common_name: Serr English Walnut (Vigorous Early-Bearing Precocious Walnut)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Serr bears young and heavily, so stake and thin a portion of the first crops to avoid limb breakage.

directions: Serr was released by the University of California in the 1960s as a fast-growing, notably precocious walnut cultivar that begins bearing at a younger age than older selections such as Franquette. Large, thin-shelled nuts with good kernel quality are borne in clusters on vigorous wood, and heavy early crops sometimes need thinning or extra bracing to prevent limbs from breaking under the weight. It leafs out fairly early in spring, so it is best sited away from frost pockets where late freezes could damage new growth and flowers. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and harvest as hulls begin to split in early fall.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Walnut Production Manual
California Walnut Board
UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research & Information Center

common_name: Payne English Walnut (Early-Leafing Precocious Heavy Bearer)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, ideally on a site with reduced spring frost risk since Payne leafs out and blooms unusually early.

directions: Payne is a long-established California walnut cultivar prized for extremely precocious, heavy bearing on a comparatively small, spreading tree, making it a popular choice for higher-density plantings. Its very early leafing and bloom give it a long growing season and abundant clustered nuts, but the same trait leaves flowers vulnerable to spring frost in colder or frost-prone sites. Nuts are medium-sized with a light-colored, good-flavored kernel, though the thin shell can be more prone to insect damage than tougher-shelled cultivars. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and away from low frost pockets, and harvest as hulls split in early fall.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Walnut Production Manual
California Walnut Board
UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research & Information Center

planting.note: Plant a grafted male tree in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun as a pollen source for female pistachio cultivars such as 'Kerman', at a ratio of roughly one male to every eight to ten female trees.

directions: Randy is a male pistachio selection grown solely as a pollen source, bearing no nuts itself but shedding pollen earlier than the older standard male cultivar 'Peters', which helps it better overlap with the bloom of widely planted female cultivars like Kerman. Site male trees evenly through a planting, or in a block upwind of prevailing spring winds, so pollen reaches female trees efficiently. Culture is identical to fruiting pistachio: deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and good heat during the growing season, with minimal water once established since pistachio is notably drought tolerant. Prune to an open form in early years to establish strong scaffold branches, since the tree needs no fruit-thinning attention.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Pistachio Production Manual
California Pistachio Research Board
UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research & Information Center

common_name: Champion Quince (Large Late-Blooming American Heirloom Quince)

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Champion blooms later than many quince selections, which helps its flowers dodge late spring frosts.

directions: Champion is a nineteenth-century American quince selection valued for large, smooth, golden-yellow fruit and heavy, reliable production on a compact, self-fruitful tree. Its late bloom period helps flowers escape the late frosts that can wipe out a quince crop in colder springs, and the mild, less astringent flesh cooks down into fragrant preserves, paste, and baked dishes with less added sugar than sharper quince cultivars need. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and prune lightly in winter to maintain an open framework and good air circulation, which reduces fire blight risk. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit turns fully golden and gives off its characteristic floral aroma.
sources: USDA National Plant Germplasm System
North American Fruit Explorers
Michael Dirr, Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; like other medlars, Monstrueuse is self-fertile and needs no second tree to fruit.

directions: Monstrueuse is an old French cultivar selected for producing some of the largest fruit of any medlar, on a small, picturesque, twisting tree that also carries showy white spring flowers and good fall color. Fruit is picked hard in late fall and then bletted, meaning it is stored in a cool spot for several weeks until the flesh softens and browns into a soft, spiced-apple-and-date flavor before eating. The tree needs little pruning beyond removing crossing or dead wood and tolerates poor soil far better than most orchard fruit, though it fruits best with a reasonably sunny site. Because it is self-fertile, a single tree will set a full crop without a pollinizer.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society
North American Fruit Explorers
Morton, J. Fruits of Warm Climates

common_name: Shinsui Asian Pear (Early Red-Skinned Juicy Nashi)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; plant a second Asian or European pear cultivar nearby for cross-pollination, since Shinsui is only partially self-fruitful.

directions: Shinsui is a Japanese-bred Asian pear valued for ripening earlier than most nashi cultivars, giving gardeners a russet-bronze, red-blushed fruit with exceptionally juicy, sweet, crisp flesh well ahead of the main late-summer pear harvest. The tree bears young and reliably, and thinning developing fruit clusters to one or two pears per spur improves final fruit size. Grow it exactly as other Asian pears, in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, with a compatible pollinizer such as Hosui or Kosui planted nearby. Pick fruit when it releases easily from the spur and the background skin color has turned from green to bronze, since unlike European pears, Asian pears ripen fully on the tree.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Pear Fruit Facts
University of California Cooperative Extension
Washington State University Extension — Asian Pear Varieties

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Monterey blooms later than Nonpareil and needs a compatible pollinizer such as Nonpareil or Carmel planted nearby.

directions: Monterey is a California-bred almond cultivar developed as a heavy-yielding, large-kerneled companion to Nonpareil, valued for its bigger nut size and later bloom that reduces frost risk compared with earlier-flowering cultivars. The soft-shelled nuts are attractive and uniform, making them popular for the in-shell and snack market as well as shelled use. It is not self-fertile and depends on overlapping bloom with a compatible pollinizer for a full crop, so orchard rows typically alternate Monterey with Nonpareil or another midseason cultivar. Grow it in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with the low water needs typical of almond, and harvest by shaking the tree once hulls split in late summer to early fall.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Almond Production Manual
Almond Board of California
UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research & Information Center
